statement: The relationship between Maya script and earlier Mesoamerican traditions (Olmec-associated symbols, Zapotec script) is unresolved, not a settled linear derivation. The "mother culture" (Olmec as single ancestral source) vs. "sister cultures" (multiple simultaneous, mutually-influencing regional developments) debate, documented by Kent V. Flannery and Joyce Marcus (University of Michigan) and David C. Grove (University of Illinois) for Mesoamerican archaeology generally, extends to writing specifically: the pre-2006 assumption of Maya writing deriving from an earlier Olmec or Zapotec source is complicated by the 2005-2006 San Bartolo discovery, which shows a mature, fully developed Maya script by c. 300-200 BCE with no obvious transitional forms linking back to Olmec symbols — leading several scholars to regard Maya writing as plausibly a separate "homegrown" development. The macro-level claim that Mesoamerican writing as a whole developed with no Old World contact is on much firmer ground than any micro-level claim about which Mesoamerican tradition gave rise to which other.
scholarly_disagreement: "Mother culture" (Olmec-derived) vs. "sister cultures" (independent regional development) framings both have named proponents and neither is settled for the specific case of script derivation.

sources.citation: Saturno, William A., David Stuart, and Boris Beltrán. "Early Maya Writing at San Bartolo, Guatemala." Science 311(5765), 2006: 1281-1283.
